notes:
Researched: Zendesk Intelligent Triage (intent + 5-point sentiment + language + per-field confidence; the "Escalate" workflow keys on billing-topic AND Very Negative sentiment; intent is set from the first customer comment, a documented mis-routing source), Intercom/Fin AI category detection (the product feature IS literally "define an attribute and describe each value in natural language" = a Choice with per-option criteria), Instructor's single- and multi-label ticket cookbooks, Banking77 (77 leaves, verbatim label names) and CLINC150 (150 in-scope + 1,200 near-miss out-of-scope), CLAMBER (ACL 2024) and "Knowing but Not Showing" (arXiv 2605.25284) 7-type ambiguity taxonomy, BFCL's Function Irrelevance Detection, litellm PR #41695's production issue-classifier, and the Jev classification_using_confidence / hierarchical_classification / date_extraction / pre_parsed_value_extraction / parallel_questions cookbooks plus the jev-1.13 jaggedness page.

Eleven transpiler rules this domain forces, most to least load-bearing:

1. MULTI-LABEL IS N NOULS, NEVER A CHOICE. Any prompt whose schema has a LIST field ("labels": [...], "missing": [...]) cannot compile to a Choice: Choice probabilities are mutually exclusive and sum to 1, so it would pick one winner and silently drop the rest. K labels -> K independent Nouls with a per-label threshold. Detect this from the output schema's array-ness, before looking at the wording. Two fixtures turn on it (instructor-multilabel-is-n-nouls, underspecified-request-clarification-gate).

2. ONE CHOICE ANSWER SATISFIES THREE PROMPT FIELDS. Prompts routinely ask for {label, second_choice, confident} or {intent, confidence}. Emit ONE Choice: `choice` + argmax of the remaining `probabilities` + `confidence`. Emitting three questions is the naive-transpiler bug. Corollary: a prompt begging "be honest about confidence" / "drop confidence below 0.5 so the router escalates" is asking for something a generated float cannot supply and a Choice supplies natively.

3. CAVEATS ARE QUESTIONS, NOT PROSE. Every "we got burned by X" paragraph is either (a) a boundary -> move into criteria.true/.false or the option description, or (b) a second judgment -> emit another Noul. "Angry is not the same as leaving" -> churn_risk criteria. "You keep giving us the previous good order" -> a separate `contrast_order` Choice. "Customers saying thanks doesn't mean resolved" -> original_issue_resolved.criteria.false. Rule (b) is the higher-value one: it converts an invisible hoped-for rule into a countable observable.

4. POLICY AND ARITHMETIC ARE RESIDUALS, NOT QUESTIONS. Thresholds ("enterprise starts at 3 minimum"), tiebreaks ("pick the queue that owns the money unless they ask to return"), compositions ("needs_confirmation = destructive OR guessed"), and all date math belong in emitted code. jev-1.13's own jaggedness page mandates this for dates and numbers. Test: if the instruction contains a number, a boolean operator, or the word "unless", it is code.

5. COLLAPSED BOOLEANS MUST BE DECOMPOSED. `needs_template` = three facts ORed together; emit has_version + has_repro_steps + has_logs and compose in code, so a mislabel tells you WHICH check fired and a template change is a one-line edit.

6. VERBATIM EXTRACTION -> CODE-SIDE CANDIDATE FINDER + CHOICE OVER THE SPANS. "Copy it exactly, don't strip the prefix, don't reformat" is an entire class of caveat that becomes unreachable once the options ARE the regex matches. Same move resolves agent-command target ids. Always add a `none` escape.

7. ORDERED BANDS ARE SCORES; UNORDERED SETS ARE CHOICES. p0..p3, small/medium/large, Very Negative..Very Positive (Zendesk's 5-point scale maps exactly onto levels 0..4). Score's between-levels answer is the honest output for a genuinely split case, and score lives in LEVEL-INDEX space (5 levels -> 0.0..4.0), so every threshold the prompt wrote as 1-5 or p0-p3 must be rewritten into index space.

8. TWO QUESTIONS, SAME TAXONOMY, DIFFERENT STATE PATHS. "initial_intent from the first message, current_intent from the latest" is where one LLM call fails worst -- scoping leaks in a single forward pass. Jev evaluates each question independently against the same state, so backtick paths (`messages[0].text`) make the scoping structural. This single pattern is the cleanest demonstration of independence.

9. STAGED CHOICE ONLY WHEN THE OPTIONS DON'T EXIST YET. A second request is justified only when the level-1 answer determines the level-2 option set (hierarchical_classification). Every other "then check whether..." belongs in the first request as speculative fan-out. Also emit a NONE_FIT / AMBIGUOUS option at each level so low confidence re-descends the runner-up branch instead of firing a wrong macro.

10. NEAR-MISS ROUTING NEEDS A CODE-SIDE GATE, NOT A BETTER-CALIBRATED CHOICE. CLINC150's out-of-scope cases are where classifiers fail. Instead of exhorting "oos is a real answer", emit a narrow literal Noul (`answerable_from_account_data`) and route on it regardless of the Choice. Include a deliberate distractor probe (`mentions_money` -> ~1.0 while routing goes the other way) to show the team the surface feature isn't driving the route.

11. NAME THE RESIDUAL OUT LOUD. Jev never emits a string, so `reasoning`, `clarifying_question`, `route`, and any summary field are undecidable and the transpiler must report them as a first-class residual: the decomposition decides WHETHER and WHICH-SLOTS, and a template or generative model writes the sentence from those flags afterwards. Three fixtures carry one.

On the corpus itself: 7 of 12 fixtures assert an UPPER bound on confidence or a wide score band, because the interesting cases are the split ones (billing-vs-returns, TOPUP-vs-CARD, streaming-vs-proxy_server, 2FA-as-account_management-vs-technical_support, spending_history-vs-oos). Where I expect Jev to be MORE decisive than a careful human -- the pronoun referent in agent-command-referent-disambiguation, and `label_billing` in the Instructor case whose published expected output is [ACCOUNT, BILLING] -- I predicted against the published answer on purpose so verification measures the miscalibration rather than hiding it. Parallel-advantage counts per request: 7, 4, 2, 5, 8, 6, 8, 9, 5, 5, 7, 6 questions; every one of those is a separate LLM call or a mega-prompt field in today's version.
verification_summary:
12/12 fixtures returned HTTP 200 on the first attempt; the documented contract was exactly right, so there are no request-validation findings to report. All responses came back `model: jev-1.13.0`. Zero drops, 3 fixtures held fully (support-triage, banking77-level2, pre-parsed-order-id), 9 needed threshold recalibration. Across 72 answers Jev emitted not one string outside the three answer shapes, confirming that `reasoning`, `clarifying_question` and `route` are genuinely uncompilable residuals.

MISCALIBRATION — the good news is there is essentially none of the dangerous kind. The one genuine label miss is `agent-command-referent-disambiguation`: I predicted rollback_migration/mig_204 on recency; Jev returned rollback_deployment/dep_8841. But it was NOT confidently wrong — target_id confidence was 0.23, the lowest in the batch, with mass split dep_8841 0.42 / AMBIGUOUS 0.29 / mig_204 0.27, and `referent_is_ambiguous` came back 0.68. Jev's system-level behaviour ("I don't know, ask the user") is correct even though its argmax is contestable; the pragmatic reading it took (you roll back the broken thing, and "ok" closes the migration topic) is defensible. Note also that tool and target stayed class-consistent (rollback_deployment paired with a dep_ id), which is the structural win that splitting one rollback tool into two was supposed to buy. The fixture is worth keeping, but asserting a specific referent there is asserting noise — assert the confirmation gate instead.

The real systematic error runs the other way: I under-predicted Jev's confidence almost everywhere. Seven of nine adjustments are `confidence_lte` assertions that had to be flipped to `confidence_gte`. Well-written, mutually exclusive criteria collapse the distribution far harder than a human reading the same surface cues expects. The extreme case is banking77 level-1: CARD came back 0.00 despite "I added money using my Visa", because TOPUP's criteria explicitly absorbed "top up by card ... or the charge for topping up". Same story for primary_label (ACCOUNT 1.00), queue (billing 1.00), provider (bedrock 1.00). The practical consequence is blunt: confidence-as-route-to-a-human is not a reliable product mechanism for a well-specified taxonomy. It only earns its keep where the option criteria genuinely overlap.

USEFULLY LOW CONFIDENCE, exactly where it should be: banking77 leaf 0.64 with 0.67/0.33 across top_up_by_card_charge and pending_top_up (the two real leaves — the beam is justified); litellm `priority` 0.54 with levels 2 and 3 splitting 0.54/0.45, i.e. a literal "between p2 and p3" and a flat refusal of the reporter's p0 claim; ambiguity_type 0.62 (temporal 0.67 / scope 0.26 — correctly refusing to peak on a taxonomy whose categories overlap); current_intent 0.69; topic_legible 0.61 on the ASR transcript. So confidence is informative precisely on the questions whose option sets are genuinely contested, and uninformative elsewhere.

STRONGEST STRUCTURAL RESULT — the multi-label proof, from one request over identical state: BILLING as a Choice option scored 0.00 while BILLING as a Noul scored 0.89. A Choice over labels provably destroys the second label. Multi-label must compile to N Nouls, never to one Choice. Three more claims confirmed empirically: path-scoping does not leak (initial_intent held order_status at 1.00 with billing content sitting later in the same state, while current_intent went billing_dispute 0.73); negation reads cleanly (excluded_weekday = Friday at 1.00, and Wednesday at exactly 0.00 on the "names first as acceptable" tiebreak); self-correction survives an agent echo (voice topic billing = 0.00 even though billing was the caller's first stated reason and the agent repeated it back). Every hard-won prompt caveat moved into criteria worked: "angry != leaving" (churn 0.97 on real signals), "not the provider they moved away from" (anthropic 0.00), "thanks is not resolution" (0.93), the ignore-the-reporter's-p0 instruction.

LATENCY: 710–1018 ms, median ~790 ms, and remarkably flat. The 9-question litellm call (1217 input tokens) took 823 ms; the 5-question multilabel call (597 input tokens) took 892 ms; the 4-choice extraction call that emitted 564 output tokens took 722 ms. Wall time is not a function of question count, state size, or option count in this range.

TRANSPILER IMPLICATIONS for this domain: (1) Fan out aggressively — 7–9 questions cost the same wall time as 2, so every "then also check whether..." belongs in the FIRST request; only a genuine option-set dependency (level-2 leaf) earns a second call. (2) Stop generating `confidence_lte` assertions for well-specified taxonomies; default to `confidence_gte` and reserve mid-band expectations for deliberately overlapping option sets. (3) Ordered bands are Scores and legitimately land between levels (measured 3.09, 0.58, 1.75, 2.44, 1.08, 0.98) — every threshold written on a prompt's 1–5 or p0–p3 scale must be rewritten into level-index space. (4) "Extract X verbatim" compiles to a code-side candidate finder plus a Choice with a `none` escape; that fixture was the cheapest and most decisive in the batch. (5) One assertion-vocabulary gap worth closing: the referent fixture needs "choice ∈ {set}" and a bare `confidence_lte` with no label, which the current expectation DSL cannot express.

fixtures.title: Support ticket triage: queue + urgency + sentiment + churn risk + refund/return intent in one request
fixtures.provenance: Zendesk Intelligent Triage — 'Automatically classifying customer intent, sentiment, and language' (support.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/4550640560538), which ships intent + a 5-point sentiment scale (Very Positive/Positive/Neutral/Negative/Very Negative) + a per-field confidence; and 'Intelligent triage use cases and workflows' (articles/5222280338202), whose documented 'Escalate' workflow keys on billing-topic AND Very Negative sentiment. Churn-signal rules (competitor mention, renewal proximity, 'evaluating alternatives') from Supportbench, 'Using AI to Detect Renewal Risk in Support Conversations' (supportbench.com/using-ai-detect-renewal-risk-support-conversations).
fixtures.llm_prompt:
You are our support triage assistant. Read the ticket below (subject + all customer messages + the account record) and return ONLY a JSON object -- no markdown fences, no commentary -- with exactly these keys:

{"queue": "billing"|"returns"|"shipping"|"technical"|"account_access"|"other",
 "urgency": 1-5 where 5 = respond within the hour,
 "sentiment": "very_negative"|"negative"|"neutral"|"positive"|"very_positive",
 "churn_risk": true|false,
 "asked_for_human": true|false,
 "refund_requested": true|false,
 "return_requested": true|false,
 "confidence": 0.0-1.0}

Rules / things we have been burned by:
- If the customer mentions a competitor by name, or says anything about "cancelling", "not renewing", "evaluating alternatives", or brings up their contract/renewal date, set churn_risk true. Do NOT set churn_risk true just because they are angry. Angry is not the same as leaving. We over-paged the CSM team for a month because of this.
- urgency should take the plan tier in the account record into account. Enterprise tickets start at 3 minimum.
- If the ticket touches two queues, pick the one that owns the MONEY, unless the customer explicitly asks to send something back.
- asked_for_human means they explicitly asked for a person / manager / callback. Being frustrated at the bot is not the same thing.
- If you are not sure about the queue, still pick one, but drop confidence below 0.5 so the router sends it to a human instead of trusting you.
- Respond only with the JSON. I mean it. Last time you prefixed it with "Here is the JSON:" and it broke the parser at 2am.
fixtures.rationale: Seven judgments that a real Zendesk triage step needs, in ONE request instead of seven LLM calls or one mega-prompt whose rules fight each other. Three things the LLM prompt does badly and the decomposition fixes: (1) The 'angry != leaving' caveat is a paragraph of pleading in the prompt; here it is churn_risk.criteria.true/.false, which is exactly the knob you turn when the CSM team gets over-paged. (2) 'Enterprise tickets start at 3 minimum' is arithmetic bolted onto a semantic judgment -- the Score measures reply pressure only, and the plan-tier floor becomes max(urgency_level, 2) in code where it can be unit-tested. (3) 'If two queues, pick the one that owns the MONEY unless they ask to send something back' is a tiebreak rule, not a classification; refund_requested and return_requested are asked independently so code owns the tiebreak. The ticket is deliberately a hard case: it straddles billing and returns, so queue.confidence should land in the middle band rather than at 1.0, and that number is the router's existing 'send to a human' gate -- the LLM prompt has to beg for it ('drop confidence below 0.5') and gets a made-up number instead. Note the Score levels run 0..4, so every threshold the prompt wrote on its 1-5 urgency scale has to be rewritten into level-index space by the transpiler.

fixtures.title: Banking77: level-1 group choice, where second_choice and confident fall out of one answer for free
fixtures.provenance: PolyAI/banking77 (huggingface.co/datasets/PolyAI/banking77; Casanueva et al., 'Efficient Intent Detection with Dual Sentence Encoders', NLP4ConvAI 2020) -- 13,083 real customer queries over 77 fine-grained banking intents. Staged-choice structure per the Jev hierarchical_classification cookbook (docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification).
fixtures.llm_prompt:
Classify the customer's message into one of our top-level support areas so the router can pick the right sub-model. Our 77 fine-grained intents (card_arrival, top_up_failed, wrong_exchange_rate_for_cash_withdrawal, pending_transfer, ...) are far too many to put in one prompt -- we tried and accuracy tanked badly on the near-duplicate ones -- so just give me the group.

Groups: CARD, TRANSFER, TOPUP, IDENTITY, FX_FEES, ACCOUNT, OTHER

Output format, nothing else:
{"group": "<GROUP>", "second_choice": "<GROUP>", "confident": true|false}

Give second_choice as well, because when you're not confident the router runs both sub-models and merges. Set confident=false if it is genuinely between two groups -- we would much rather run two cheap sub-models than route to the wrong one.
fixtures.rationale: The LLM prompt asks for three fields; a Choice answer already contains all three and the transpiler should emit ONE question, not three. `group` is `choice`, `second_choice` is the argmax of `probabilities` minus the winner, and `confident` is a threshold on `confidence` -- no extra tokens, and unlike the LLM version the second choice is a real ranked runner-up rather than a plausible-sounding guess. The three Nouls ride along for free and are the ones that actually let code skip the level-2 request: the message is a fee dispute AND a pending transaction, which in Banking77 are two different leaves (top_up_by_card_charge vs pending_top_up), so `two_distinct_issues` is what tells the router to split the ticket instead of picking a loser. I predict a mid-band confidence here rather than a peak, because TOPUP and CARD both have real pull ('added money using my Visa'); that is the honest answer and the reason the router's two-sub-model path exists at all.

group.instructions: Which top-level support area does the customer's message belong to?

criteria.CARD: The physical or virtual card itself: arrival, delivery, activation, PIN, card declined, contactless, card swallowed, lost or stolen, card not working.
criteria.TRANSFER: Money moving between accounts or to another person: outgoing transfers, incoming transfers, failed or pending transfers, transfer timing, beneficiaries.
criteria.TOPUP: Adding money into the account: top up by card, bank transfer, cash or cheque; top up failed, pending, reverted, limits, or the charge for topping up.
criteria.IDENTITY: Identity and source-of-funds verification, and personal detail changes.
criteria.FX_FEES: Exchange rates and the fees or charges applied to exchange and cash withdrawal.
criteria.ACCOUNT: Account-level matters: closing or terminating the account, age or country eligibility, supported cards and currencies.
criteria.OTHER: None of the above groups fits.

pending_status.instructions: Does the customer say a transaction has not completed yet -- pending, still processing, or not arrived?

fee_dispute.instructions: Does the customer dispute or question a fee, charge, or exchange rate?

two_distinct_issues.instructions: Does the message raise two distinct problems that different teams would handle, rather than one problem described twice?

criteria.true: Two separable problems, each of which would still be a ticket on its own.
criteria.false: One problem, even if the customer describes several symptoms of it.

measured.notes: Label correct, but confidence_lte 0.85 failed hard: measured 1.00 with CARD at exactly 0.00 and every other group at 0.00. My prediction that 'TOPUP and CARD both have real pull' was wrong, and the reason is instructive -- TOPUP's criteria explicitly enumerate 'top up by card ... or the charge for topping up', so the Visa mention is absorbed rather than contested. Good criteria collapse the distribution. Practical consequence: the two-sub-model beam path this fixture was meant to justify would never trigger from group.confidence on this message. What DOES justify splitting the ticket is two_distinct_issues at 0.74, which is the honest middling answer and the signal code should actually route on. Both ride-along Nouls are near-saturated (0.98/0.98), correctly identifying the fee dispute and the pending transaction as separate Banking77 leaves. The three-fields-from-one-Choice claim holds mechanically, but second_choice is degenerate here: every runner-up is 0.00, so argmax-minus-winner returns an arbitrary tie rather than a ranked alternative. The transpiler should treat second_choice as valid only when runner-up probability clears a floor.

primary_complaint_is_the_fee.instructions: Is the unrecognised fee the customer's main complaint, rather than the delay?

fixtures.provenance: Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL), UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab -- specifically its Function Relevance / Irrelevance Detection category (875 cases where none of the provided functions should be invoked) and its multi-turn trajectory evaluation (sky.cs.berkeley.edu/project/berkeley-function-calling-leaderboard). fixtures.llm_prompt:
You are the intent resolver sitting in front of our ops agent. The user just typed something. Below you get the last turns of the conversation and the tools the agent has.

Decide which tool the user wants called and which object they mean. Reply with JSON only:
{"tool": "<tool name or NONE>", "target_id": "<id from the conversation or NONE>", "needs_confirmation": true|false, "reasoning": "<one sentence>"}

Important:
- Return "NONE" for tool if nothing fits. Do NOT force a tool. We had an incident where you picked rollback_deployment for "what happened here?" and it rolled back prod.
- needs_confirmation must be true for anything destructive (rollback, delete, scale down, revoke) OR if you had to guess which target they meant.
- When the user says "that" / "it" / "the last one", resolve it against the conversation. If two things could plausibly be "it", set needs_confirmation true and still put your best guess in target_id.
- target_id must be copied verbatim from the conversation. Do not reconstruct it from memory, we have seen dep_8841 come back as dep_8481.
fixtures.rationale: The transpiler's job here is to notice that 'which tool' and 'which object' are two closed sets, not one JSON blob, and that the candidate ids must come from code -- a regex over the transcript -- so the answer is a verbatim copy of a real id and the prompt's 'dep_8841 came back as dep_8481' failure becomes structurally unreachable. BFCL's irrelevance category is the NONE option, and splitting rollback into rollback_deployment / rollback_migration forces the tool answer to be consistent with the target class instead of letting a mega-prompt emit rollback_deployment(mig_204). needs_confirmation is NOT a question: it is `is_destructive OR referent_is_ambiguous OR NOT user_stated_target_explicitly`, evaluated in code, which is where a confirmation policy belongs and where it can be tightened after an incident without touching a prompt. Residual the transpiler must report as undecidable: `reasoning` is free text and Jev never generates text -- drop it, or route just that field to a generative model AFTER the decision is made, so the explanation can never change the decision. I predict mig_204 on recency (the user asked about the migration one turn earlier) with deliberately non-peaked confidence, and a genuinely middling `referent_is_ambiguous` -- this is a case where I expect Jev to read the pronoun more decisively than a careful human would, and if it does, that miscalibration is exactly what this fixture should expose.

messages.text: Two things. Deploy dep_8841 (api-gateway, rolled 14:02) is failing health checks on 3 of 8 pods. Deploy dep_8839 (billing-worker, rolled 13:47) is up but throwing a 6% error rate.

criteria.scale_service: Change the replica count of a service.

criteria.NONE: The user is not asking for any of these tools -- they are commenting, asking a general question, or asking something no listed tool can do.

criteria.dep_8841: The api-gateway deployment rolled at 14:02 that is failing health checks.
criteria.dep_8839: The billing-worker deployment rolled at 13:47 with a 6% error rate.
criteria.mig_204: The database migration that is 60% through.

criteria.false: The conversation makes exactly one referent the obvious reading.

Jev's reading is defensible -- 'ok' plausibly closes the migration topic, and you roll back the thing that is broken, not the migration running clean at 60%. A careful human would also hesitate, which is precisely what 0.23 and 0.68 encode. Two structural claims confirmed: tool and target stayed class-consistent (rollback_deployment with a dep_ id, never rollback_deployment(mig_204)), and the NONE/irrelevance option stayed at 0.02 without suppressing a real tool pick. The composed policy is correct regardless of the argmax -- is_destructive 0.94 OR referent_is_ambiguous 0.68 OR NOT user_stated_target_explicitly 0.06 all independently force confirmation, so no rollback fires unconfirmed. ADJUSTMENT RATIONALE: asserting any single referent here is asserting noise, so the corrected expectation drops the target_id label and asserts only that confidence stays low. That exposes a gap in the assertion DSL -- this fixture wants 'choice in {rollback_deployment, rollback_migration}' and a bare confidence bound with no label; recommend adding choice_in. Before we answer the user, decide whether to answer or to ask a clarifying question first. Return JSON:

{"needs_clarification": true|false,

Guidance: only ask when you genuinely cannot proceed. Users hate being interrogated and we get complaints about it. If there is an obvious default interpretation -- the most common one, or the one implied by the rest of the conversation -- answer and state your assumption instead of asking. fixtures.rationale: The central transpiler lesson: the prompt's `missing: [...]` is a LIST, and a Choice cannot produce a list -- its probabilities are mutually exclusive and sum to 1, so a Choice over slots would force one winner and silently hide the other two gaps. Second lesson: 'only ask when you genuinely cannot proceed / users hate being interrogated' is a POLICY, not a judgment. Transpile it into `needs_clarification` (the judgment) plus `cost_of_guessing_wrong` (the stakes) and let code own the threshold, so tuning how chatty the agent is becomes a constant instead of a prompt rewrite. Residual the transpiler must report: `clarifying_question` is generated text and Jev cannot produce it -- the decomposition decides WHETHER to ask and WHICH slots are missing, and a template or a generative model writes the sentence from those flags. I predict `ambiguity_type` comes back with spread rather than a peak (temporal and scope both genuinely apply to 'churn numbers' with no window), which is why the assertion is on confidence and not on a label: forcing a single ambiguity type is the published taxonomy's weakness, not Jev's, and a low confidence here is the correct answer rather than a failure.

fixtures.llm_prompt:
Extract the order number the customer is complaining about from the email below. Output JSON: {"order_number": "<string>", "confidence": 0.0-1.0}

Notes, all of which we learned the hard way:
- The email may contain several numbers: a case number from our own autoresponder in the subject line, a carrier tracking number, an invoice number, and the customer's membership number. We only want the ORDER number.
- Specifically the one the complaint is ABOUT. Customers very often reference a previous good order to contrast with the bad one, and you keep giving us the good one.
- Copy it EXACTLY as written. Do not reformat, do not strip the ORD- prefix, do not helpfully remove the dashes.
- If there is no order number at all, return null. Do not return the case number instead.
fixtures.rationale: Every caveat in the LLM prompt is a symptom of asking a generative model to emit a string. 'Copy it EXACTLY, do not strip the prefix, do not remove the dashes' disappears entirely once the options ARE the regex spans: the answer is an index into a list code already owns, so code copies the span and a transposed digit is not a reachable state. 'You keep giving us the good one' is not a caveat either -- it is a second question. Asking `contrast_order` alongside `complaint_order` turns the trap into an assertion you can regression-test, and the two answers must differ or something is wrong. Then the tracking and invoice picks, plus two Nouls the downstream macro needs, ride along in the same request: six answers where the prompt-and-parse version produced one brittle string. The transpiler rule to extract: when a prompt says 'extract X verbatim', emit a code-side candidate finder plus a Choice over its output with a `none` escape, and never a question that asks for X itself. This is also the only fixture where I predict high confidence across the board, which is the point -- once the answer space is the right shape, the easy cases become genuinely easy.

fixtures.provenance: Jev date_extraction cookbook (docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook) -- seven Choice questions read mode/month/day/year/day_anchor/weekday/week_offset off the text and code resolves them to a date, with a fixed reference 'today' and confidence gating for human review; plus the documented jev-1.13 failure modes 'Math and Numbers' and 'Date and time comparison' (docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13), which state outright that date ordering and arithmetic must stay in code.

The customer said 'Tuesday or Wednesday', which the LLM prompt's schema literally cannot hold -- it papers over that with 'just pick the earliest' and returns a single date that looks certain. The Noul surfaces that a range was offered, so the scheduler can book a two-day window or offer both slots instead of silently discarding half the customer's answer. kind.instructions: What kind of issue is this?

criteria.bug: Something documented does not work as described.
criteria.feature: A request for behaviour that does not exist yet.
criteria.docs: The code is correct but the documentation is wrong, missing, or misleading.
criteria.question: The reporter wants help using the project, not a code change.

domain.instructions: Which subsystem owns this issue? Judge from the described behaviour, not from which provider is named.

criteria.streaming: Server-sent events, chunk assembly, stream lifecycle and termination.
criteria.proxy_server: The proxy process itself: routing of requests, workers, timeouts, connection handling.
criteria.router: Model fallbacks, load balancing, retries across deployments.
criteria.sdk_client: The client library surface, not the proxy.
criteria.unknown: The issue does not give enough to attribute a subsystem.

provider.instructions: Which LLM provider is the reported problem happening on? If two providers are named, choose the one the failure occurs on, not one the reporter moved away from.

criteria.other: A provider not in this list is named.

priority.instructions: How severe is this issue, judged from the described impact? Ignore `priority_claimed_by_reporter`.
criteria: Cosmetic, documentation-only, or a question; nothing is broken.
A feature is degraded or broken but a documented workaround exists.
A documented feature is broken with no workaround, for a real class of users.
Data loss, a security problem, or total outage of a documented feature.

lift.instructions: How much engineering effort would fixing this take?
criteria: Small: a localized change in one place, plus a test.
Medium: changes across a few modules, or needs a reproduction harness first.
Large: requires design work, touches an interface, or spans several subsystems.

has_repro_steps.instructions: Does `body` give steps another engineer could follow to reproduce the problem?

criteria.true: There is a concrete sequence, request, or configuration that would trigger the behaviour.
criteria.false: The behaviour is described but not the steps that produce it.

has_version.instructions: Does `body` state which version of the project the reporter is running?

fixtures.title: Multi-label support ticket categorization is N Nouls, not one Choice
fixtures.provenance: Instructor documentation, 'Multi-Label Classification -- Support Ticket Categorization' (python.useinstructor.com/examples/multiple_classification/): system message 'You are a support agent at a tech company. fixtures.llm_prompt:
You are a support agent at a tech company. Only select the labels that apply to the support ticket.

Labels: ACCOUNT, BILLING, GENERAL_QUERY

Return {"labels": ["..."]} -- a list, because a ticket can have more than one. Only include labels that actually apply; don't pad the list to look thorough. Don't invent labels that aren't in the list above. If none apply, return an empty list.
fixtures.rationale: This is the structural rule the transpiler most needs and most easily gets wrong: multi-label does NOT compile to a Choice. A Choice returns a probability distribution that sums to 1 over mutually exclusive options, so a Choice over {ACCOUNT, BILLING, GENERAL_QUERY} can never say 'both' -- it would return ACCOUNT at 0.6 and BILLING at 0.4 and code would throw the second label away. K labels compile to K independent Nouls with a threshold per label, which also means the labels become individually tunable: if BILLING over-fires you raise its threshold or sharpen its criteria without touching ACCOUNT, whereas in the LLM version every label shares one prompt and one blast radius. 'Don't pad the list' and 'don't invent labels that aren't in the list' both become unreachable rather than requested -- there is no list to pad and no string to invent. The `primary_label` Choice rides along free for the router that needs a single owner, so one request yields both multi-label and single-label semantics. My honest prediction is the interesting part: Instructor's docs give [ACCOUNT, BILLING] as the expected output, but the ticket's actual PROBLEM is the lockout and billing info is only what the customer cannot reach -- so I predict label_billing lands well above 0 but below a confident yes. That is exactly the calibration a threshold exists to exploit, and exactly what a one-shot list output hides.

fixtures.title: Out-of-scope detection: refusing to map a near-miss request onto the nearest intent
fixtures.provenance: CLINC150 -- Larson et al., 'An Evaluation Dataset for Intent Classification and Out-of-Scope Prediction', EMNLP 2019: 23,700 queries, 22,500 in-scope over 150 intents across 10 domains, plus 1,200 deliberately out-of-scope queries constructed to sit near in-scope ones. Confidence-gated fallback per docs.typesafe.ai/confidence and the classification_using_confidence cookbook, whose measured finding is that a 0.9 cutoff splits 60 filings in half with 90% accuracy above it and 40% below.
fixtures.llm_prompt:
Classify the user's utterance into one of our supported intents. If the utterance is not something our assistant supports at all, return "oos".

Intents: balance, transfer, pay_bill, card_declined, report_lost_card, freeze_account, exchange_rate, spending_history, update_address, oos

Return {"intent": "...", "confidence": 0.0-1.0}.

Be honest about confidence. We drop anything under 0.7 into the out-of-scope bucket and hand it to a human, and we would rather do that than answer the wrong question. Do NOT map a request onto the nearest intent just because it is the nearest -- "oos" is a real answer and you should use it. Most of our bad escalations come from you confidently picking spending_history for anything that mentions money.
fixtures.rationale: CLINC150's out-of-scope split exists precisely because near-miss utterances are where intent classifiers fail, and this is one: it mentions money and a month, which is the exact surface shape of spending_history, but what it asks for is an insurer's price change, which the bank does not hold. The LLM prompt tries to fix that with two paragraphs of exhortation ('oos is a real answer', 'most of our bad escalations come from you confidently picking spending_history'), which is unfalsifiable -- you cannot regression-test a plea. The decomposition makes it a testable gate: `answerable_from_account_data` is a narrow, literal question with an explicit boundary in its criteria, and code routes to oos when it is false NO MATTER what the Choice said. The oos decision therefore stops depending on a Choice being well calibrated over a near-miss, which is the thing that was actually failing. `mentions_money` is in there as a deliberate distractor probe: it should come back near 1 while the route goes the other way, which is how you show the team that surface money-mentions are not driving the decision. I am predicting intent = oos with non-peaked confidence and I may well be wrong -- spending_history is a genuinely strong attractor here -- and that is the point: if Jev picks spending_history, the code-side gate still routes correctly, and the fixture will have measured a real miscalibration instead of hiding it behind a hedge.

fixtures.title: Intent set from the first message only: detecting that the thread has moved on
fixtures.provenance: Zendesk help, 'Making sense of unexpected intelligent triage predictions' (support.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/5608698604698) -- intelligent triage predicts intent from the customer's comment, and unexpected predictions are a documented operational problem; plus 'Intelligent triage use cases and workflows' (articles/5222280338202), whose 'Route' and 'Reduce' workflows both key off that single prediction. State-path referencing per docs.typesafe.ai/primitives#reference-specific-fields.
fixtures.llm_prompt:
Our ticket intent is currently set from the FIRST customer comment only, and it is causing mis-routing when the conversation moves on -- the ticket stays in the shipping queue for a week while the customer is actually asking about an invoice.

Read the whole thread and return JSON:
{"initial_intent": "...", "current_intent": "...", "intent_changed": true|false,
 "should_resplit": true|false, "resolved": true|false, "who_we_are_waiting_on": "customer"|"us"}

Intents: order_status, return_request, billing_dispute, product_question, account_access, complaint, other

- initial_intent: what the FIRST customer message was about. Not the thread.
- current_intent: what the customer's LATEST message is about.
- should_resplit: true if the thread now contains a second, unrelated issue that deserves its own ticket.
- resolved: true only if the ORIGINAL issue is done. Customers saying "thanks" does not by itself mean resolved.
fixtures.rationale: Two Choice questions over the SAME taxonomy, pointed at different parts of the state by path (`messages[0].text` vs `messages[2].text`), in one request. This is the shape a single LLM call handles worst: both fields come out of one forward pass over the whole thread, so the 'judge only that message' scoping leaks and initial_intent drifts toward whatever the thread is about now -- which is precisely the mis-routing the team is trying to fix. Jev evaluates every question independently against the same state, so the scoping is structural rather than a hope, and the two answers can disagree without one contaminating the other. `intent_changed` then becomes a cross-check rather than a third guess: code can compare the two Choices AND read the Noul, and disagreement between those two routes is a signal worth logging. The prompt's hard-won caveat -- 'customers saying thanks does not by itself mean resolved' -- goes straight into original_issue_resolved.criteria.false, sitting next to the boundary it describes, and `customer_satisfied_with_handling` is asked separately so the two can never be conflated again. `who_we_are_waiting_on` becomes a positively-phrased Noul rather than a two-option Choice, because jev-1.13's contradictory-criteria failure mode says a binary Choice over 'us' vs 'them' reads worse than a direct yes/no.

fixtures.provenance: Intercom, 'Use AI category detection in Fin workflows' (fin.ai/help/en/articles/10624992) -- the documented mechanism is to define a conversation attribute and describe each of its values in natural language, i.e. a Choice with per-option criteria; and 'Deploy Fin AI Agent over phone' (intercom.com/help/en/articles/10697275), which states Fin detects which topic or issue type the call falls into (for example Billing, Account Management, Technical Support) from what the caller says. fixtures.llm_prompt:
You're classifying a phone call transcript from our voice agent. The transcript comes from ASR, so expect errors, dropped words, filler, and the caller talking over the agent.

Return JSON only:
{"topic": "billing"|"account_management"|"technical_support"|"scheduling"|"sales"|"other",
 "caller_goal": "resolve_now"|"schedule_callback"|"speak_to_human"|"information_only",
 "transcript_usable": true|false}

transcript_usable = false if the ASR is too garbled to trust the classification. If transcript_usable is false we route to a human and ignore your other two fields, so don't try to be clever -- tell us when you can't read it. Also: callers very often start with the wrong reason and then correct themselves ("no no, not that, it's the..."). Classify what they ended up asking for, not the first thing they said. We had a whole week of 2FA calls landing in the billing queue because of this.
fixtures.rationale: Intercom's AI category detection IS a Choice -- the documented way to configure it is 'define a conversation attribute and describe each of the values in natural language' -- so the topic taxonomy transpiles almost mechanically, and the interesting work is everything the prompt wraps around it. 'Classify what they ended up asking for, not the first thing they said' is a caveat carrying a whole week of mis-routed 2FA calls; splitting it into an instruction on `topic` PLUS an independent `caller_corrected_themselves` Noul means the correction becomes an observable you can count on a dashboard, not an invisible rule you hope fired. 'transcript_usable' gets rephrased as `topic_legible` and narrowed from 'is the ASR good' to 'is it good enough to route', because jev-1.13 reads instructions literally and 'usable' has no boundary -- and it is phrased positively so high means yes, per the noul guidance against inverted criteria. The prediction I am least sure of is `topic`: a 2FA login problem sits right on the account_management / technical_support line, and the criteria are written to put it in account_management, so if it comes back technical_support the criteria are what need fixing -- a far cheaper fix than a prompt rewrite, and the whole argument for criteria over prose. `frustration` rides along with a deliberately wide predicted band: a caller who was misheard twice and gave up is somewhere between levels 1 and 2, and asserting a point value there would be pretending to a precision the data does not support.
